title: Killing them with kindness
intro: A short magazine-style article about why so many houseplants die and how to keep yours alive. Tomasz is a made-up example, not a real person; the article was written for Psotek English
paras: When Tomasz moved into his first flat, he bought six plants to make it feel like home. Within two months, all six were dead. "I watered them every single day," he says. "Nobody could say I didn't care." That, it turns out, was exactly the problem. His story is very common: experts say that more houseplants die from too much attention than from too little.

The biggest killer of indoor plants is overwatering. Roots need air as well as water, and when the soil stays wet for too long, they cannot breathe. Slowly they begin to rot, and the leaves above them turn yellow and droopy. Unfortunately, a thirsty plant and a drowning plant can look almost the same, so many owners react to the warning signs by reaching for the watering can again.

Instead of following a fixed timetable, gardeners recommend a simple test. Push a finger into the soil up to the second knuckle. If it feels dry, water the plant thoroughly, until water runs out of the hole at the bottom of the pot. If it still feels damp, leave it alone and check again in a few days. A pot without a drainage hole is a trap, because the extra water has nowhere to go.

Light is the other half of the story. Every plant comes from a particular natural home, and it does best when you copy those conditions. A cactus from the desert will be happy on a sunny windowsill, while many popular leafy plants come from the shady floor of tropical forests and can burn in strong, direct sun. Before you buy a plant, it is worth reading the small label in the pot rather than choosing it only because it looks pretty.

Last spring, Tomasz decided to give plants another chance. This time he chose just two easy species, put them near a bright window and felt the soil once a week before deciding whether to water. Both are still alive, and one has even produced three new leaves. "I learned that looking after something sometimes means doing less," he says. "Now I wait until they actually need me."
